readerTitle: Why the plumber gets called before the home check-up
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 수리업 두 곳, 회사 안의 데이터팀). 실제 기업 사례로 수치를 지어내지 않으려고 company_story 대신 두 사업 비교 형식을 택함
insight: 진통제냐 비타민이냐는 제품이 정하는 것이 아니라, 고객이 지금 겪는 고통에 그 제품을 붙이느냐가 정한다.
misconception: 장기적으로 더 큰 가치를 주는 제품이 더 쉽게 팔린다. 비타민형 제품은 나쁜 사업이다.

sources.text: 'Painkiller vs vitamin'은 스타트업·투자 업계에서 널리 쓰이는 비유 (특정 연구 결과가 아님)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 'painkiller vs vitamin' 표현의 최초 출처는 불분명합니다. 카드에서 특정 인물이나 기관에 귀속하지 않았습니다. 게시 전에 귀속 문구가 없는지 다시 확인하세요.
모든 가격($180 출장 수리, 연 $180 점검 플랜)과 시간(금요일 스프레드시트 3시간)은 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산이 필요한 주장은 없습니다.

cards.title: Why the plumber gets called before the home check-up
body: Two home-service businesses open in the same town in the same month. Both charge about $180. Both are run by skilled, friendly people.
One fixes leaks and blocked drains the same day. The other offers a yearly home check-up that catches problems early.
By month three, one is turning work away. The other is still handing out flyers.

image.label: Two vans: one rushing to a flooded kitchen, one parked and idle
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 같은 거리에 밴 두 대. 왼쪽 밴은 물이 새는 부엌이 있는 집으로 급히 출발(모션 라인, 휴대폰 알림 아이콘 여러 개). 오른쪽 밴은 전단지 더미와 함께 조용히 서 있음. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which one fills its calendar first?
body: The emergency repair business: $180 per call-out, same day.
The check-up plan: $180 a year, and it could prevent repairs that cost far more.
Which gets its first 50 customers faster?

options.text: The check-up plan, because it saves customers more money over time
options.feedback: It may well deliver more value. But customers have to believe in a future problem and act before it exists, and most put that off.

options.text: The emergency repairs, because customers are already looking for help
options.feedback: A flooded kitchen creates its own urgency. The customer searches, calls and pays today. The trade-off is that each job may be one-off.
Ads matter, but they work very differently. The repair ad catches people already searching. The check-up ad has to convince people they need it at all.

cards.title: One business was found. The other had to persuade.
body: The repair business barely marketed. People with water on the floor searched, found it, and booked within minutes. Few asked about price.
The check-up business heard "great idea" at almost every door. Then people said they'd think about it. Most never called back.
Both offers were useful. Only one solved a problem the customer felt **right now**.

cards.title: Painkillers and vitamins
body: A **painkiller** solves a problem the customer feels now and is already trying to fix. A **vitamin** makes life better someday. It's nice to have, but nothing bad happens this week without it.
Painkillers get bought. Vitamins have to be sold. That difference shapes your marketing, your sales cycle and how hard customers push on price.
cards.softwareNote: In software, a quick test is what users do when your product breaks. If they complain within the hour, it's a painkiller. If nobody notices for a week, it's a vitamin.

cards.title: Signs you're selling a painkiller
body: Look at what customers do, not what they say.
list: **They already pay for a workaround:** time, money or a clumsy fix
**They come looking for you,** not the other way round
**There's a deadline:** a leak, an audit, a launch date
**Saying no has a cost they can name** this week
cards.callout: If none of these are true, you're probably selling a vitamin, even if customers say they love it.

cards.title: Same plan, different moment.
body: The two owners teamed up. Now the plumber, standing in a freshly dried kitchen, offers the check-up plan: "Want me to check the rest of the house so this doesn't happen again?"
Many say yes on the spot. The plan didn't change. The moment did. Right after a flood, prevention isn't a vitamin anymore.
Being a painkiller is less about the product and more about **which pain you attach it to**.

image.label: Plumber offering a check-up plan in a just-repaired kitchen
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 막 수리를 끝낸 부엌, 바닥에 아직 수건이 놓여 있음. 수리공이 집주인에게 클립보드("Yearly check-up")를 보여주고 집주인이 고개를 끄덕임. 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Vitamins aren't bad businesses.
body: Painkillers sell fast, but emergencies are often one-off, and desperate customers shop around next time. Many vitamins, like gyms, coffee or skincare, build habits and loyal customers who stay for years.
The risk is also in selling. Inventing or inflating pain to close a sale turns into fear-mongering, and customers notice. Find the real pain that's already there. Don't manufacture one.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: You lead a small data team at a retail company. You've built a sales dashboard, but the sales managers ignore it. Each Friday, they spend about three hours building a spreadsheet for the weekly review.
How do you pitch the dashboard?

options.text: "It gives you richer insights into your pipeline"
options.feedback: True, but it's a vitamin. Busy managers nod and keep doing what they already do.

options.text: "It builds your Friday review sheet for you, so you get those three hours back"
options.feedback: You attach the tool to a pain they already pay for every week. The cost is that you must make sure it really replaces the spreadsheet.

options.text: Ask the sales director to make it mandatory
options.feedback: You'll get logins quickly. But forced use without relief often becomes box-ticking, and the spreadsheet quietly lives on.

cards.title: Find the pain your offer already relieves.
body: Painkillers get bought, vitamins get sold. Before you change the product, try changing which pain you connect it to and when you offer it.
**Try it today:** write down what your customers did last time before they found you. Whatever they were struggling with is the pain to lead with.
